title.heading: Hadrian’s Wall
title.lead: Why do we put gates in walls?

picture.shows: A colour reconstruction of Hadrian’s Wall with a guarded gateway
picture.subject: generic

slides.heading: Hadrian orders a wall
slides.lead: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered a wall across northern Britain.
points: Its route lies in northern England today.
It ran from Wallsend near Newcastle to Bowness-on-Solway on the west coast.

cards.label: Emperor
cards.meaning: He ruled the Roman Empire when the wall was started.

figure.shows: A map of Britain showing Hadrian’s Wall from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, with the modern England–Scotland border farther north
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Why build a wall?
slides.lead: Hadrian’s Wall marked the northern frontier of Roman Britain.
points: Britons living north of the wall could raid Roman land. Soldiers on the wall could watch for danger.
Guarded crossings helped Roman soldiers control who entered Roman Britain.

cards.label: Frontier
cards.meaning: The edge of land an empire controls.

figure.shows: A reconstruction showing Roman soldiers watching the northern approach from Hadrian’s Wall
figure.subject: generic

myth.claim: Hadrian’s Wall follows the border between England and Scotland.
myth.fact: The wall is in England. Today’s border with Scotland lies north of the wall.

picture.shows: A reconstruction of a Roman fort beside Hadrian’s Wall
picture.subject: generic

items.name: Milecastles
items.text: Small forts guarded each Roman mile.

picture.shows: A reconstruction of a milecastle attached to Hadrian’s Wall
picture.subject: generic

picture.shows: A reconstruction of a guarded Roman gateway through Hadrian’s Wall
picture.subject: generic

slides.heading: A gate was a checkpoint
slides.lead: Hadrian’s Wall did not stop every journey across the frontier.
points: Gates channelled travellers into places where Roman soldiers could check them.
Soldiers could inspect goods carried through gates and collect taxes on trade.

cards.label: Trade tax
cards.meaning: Money traders paid when bringing goods across the frontier.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of Roman soldiers checking a trader and a loaded cart at a gateway in Hadrian’s Wall
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Which statement best explains how the wall helped Rome?

options.text: It helped soldiers watch for raids and check frontier crossings.
It helped soldiers defend Roman Britain by stopping every frontier crossing.
options.why: The pupil understands defence but thinks the wall prevented all movement, overlooking the gates.

options.text: It helped soldiers check frontier crossings but offered no defence against raids.
options.why: The pupil remembers checks at gates but separates control from the wall’s defensive purpose.

items.question: A trader wants to bring wool into Roman Britain. How could soldiers at a gate control this crossing?
items.answer: Soldiers could check the trader’s wool and collect a tax before letting the trader through.

items.question: A Roman officer suggests removing every gate to improve defence. Why could keeping guarded gates be a better plan?
items.answer: Guarded gates let trade continue while soldiers checked travellers and watched for danger.

items.question: When did Hadrian order his wall, and where is its route?
items.answer: In AD 122, across what is now northern England.

items.question: How could the wall help soldiers spot danger before raids arrived?
items.answer: Soldiers on the wall could watch the land to the north.

items.question: How did forts, milecastles and gates each help soldiers guard crossings?
items.answer: Forts housed soldiers for patrols, milecastles guarded each Roman mile, and gates provided places to check travellers.
